subject: 04F924E0CC51EDF12DBB02871348AD74
introduction: “He is the Rememberer and the Remembered!” These short readings, most of them openings of prayers and tablets, say one thing with great persistence: only God can describe God. From eternity He has praised and borne witness to Himself; whatever a creature says of Him stays “within the bounds” of creation. The conclusion is neither silence nor despair. The worshipper takes up the words God has used of Himself in revelation, and learns to read the signs by which “God described Himself to everything through everything,” every soul being a mirror. The thought is found wherever people have reflected on praise: in Ben Sira’s “we may speak much, and yet come short,” in the Name given at the bush, in the Qur’án’s “Allah Himself is Witness,” in Dante’s Light that knows and loves itself, in Aristotle and Spinoza, in Herbert’s line that prayer is “God’s breath in man returning to his birth.” The last psalm’s “let every thing that hath breath praise the Lord,” and Xenophanes on gods made in the image of their worshippers, raise the two questions the readings must answer. The tradition quoted in the tenth reading, “I cannot reckon Thy praise; Thou art as Thou hast praised Thyself,” could not be checked against a source page and is left as the reading gives it.
questions: “Thou art not described except by Thyself.” What follows for the way you use, and trust, your own words about God?
If only God’s praise of Himself is adequate, why does scripture command every creature to praise? What does praise do for the one who offers it?
“In all things there is a sign indicating that He is One.” Where today did you see such a sign and pass it by?
Xenophanes said that oxen would draw their gods as oxen. How does the idea that God describes Himself through revelation answer him, and where does his warning still apply?
“All souls are as mirrors.” What clouds a mirror, and what does the image ask of a person?

outside.why: “From eternity Thou didst Thyself describe Thine own Self unto Thy Self.” Dante, at the last vision of the Paradiso: O Light Eterne, sole in thyself that dwellest, sole knowest thyself, and, known unto thyself and knowing, lovest and smilest on thyself.
“Who is there besides Thee that can claim to know Thee?” Paul: the things of God knoweth no man, but the Spirit of God.
“Every name beareth witness that He is sanctified from all names.” The Levites’ call to worship admits as much: thy glorious name, which is exalted above all blessing and praise.
“I am the Witness and the Witnessed One.” The Qur’án: Allah Himself is Witness that there is no God save Him.
“He has ever been His own describer of His Self … None knoweth how He is except Him.” Asked for a name, the Voice from the bush gave one that only the speaker can say: I Am That I Am.
He “describeth His Own Self by His Self.” Aristotle reached a like thought by argument: it must be of itself that the divine thought thinks, and its thinking is a thinking on thinking.
“Ever hath Thy Reality praised Thy Reality,” and all other praise stays within created bounds. The psalmist: who can utter the mighty acts of the Lord? who can shew forth all his praise?

The Psalter nevertheless ends with a command: let every thing that hath breath praise the Lord. If only God’s praise of Himself is adequate, why are creatures asked to praise at all? What is their praise for?

“That only which is worthy of Thee is the anthem of praise voiced by Thine Own Essence.” Ben Sira: we may speak much, and yet come short. When ye glorify the Lord, exalt him as much as ye can; for even yet will he far exceed.

The worshipper falls back on “what the tongue of Thy Revelation hath spoken.” On Sinai it is God who proclaims God’s name, and Israel has repeated His words ever since: The Lord, The Lord God, merciful and gracious, longsuffering.
“The describer is the very description.” Hebrews, on why God’s witness to Himself has no other to appeal to: because he could swear by no greater, he sware by himself.

“God described Himself to everything through everything … in all things there is a sign.” Paul: the invisible things of him from the creation of the world are clearly seen, being understood by the things that are made.
The Qur’án: there is not a thing but hymneth His praise; but ye understand not their praise.
“All souls are as mirrors.” Leibniz: each simple substance is a perpetual living mirror of the universe.
To know Him otherwise than as He has revealed Himself is to be veiled. John: no man hath seen God at any time; the only begotten Son, he hath declared him.

“God testifieth of His own Self unto His own Self.” Among men the rule is the reverse, and Jesus cites it: if I bear witness of myself, my witness is not true. Why is self-testimony worthless in a human court and the only possible testimony here?
Creation “knoweth not a single letter of that testimony.” The last sentence of Wittgenstein’s Tractatus: whereof one cannot speak, thereof one must be silent.
“The Hidden Mystery.” The Tao Te Ching: the name that can be named is not the enduring and unchanging name.
“He giveth thanks unto Himself.” Spinoza came to a kindred sentence: the intellectual love of the mind towards God is that very love of God whereby God loves himself.

God speaks of His power, life and grandeur so that creatures will not doubt, though He is “not encompassed by what they have encompassed.” Xenophanes explained where human descriptions of the divine come from: horses would paint the forms of the gods like horses, and oxen like oxen. How do the readings avoid his charge?
“Thou hast been the One Who praiseth Thy Essence through Thy Essence.” George Herbert’s definition of prayer makes even ours His own: God’s breath in man returning to his birth.
Paul says something similar of prayer: we know not what we should pray for as we ought: but the Spirit itself maketh intercession for us.
A glorification “wherewith none of Thy creation hath ever glorified Thee.” The psalm: great is the Lord, and greatly to be praised; and his greatness is unsearchable.
The Sun “becomes revealed in the mirrors of existing things” according to their ranks. Paul: now we see through a glass, darkly; but then face to face.

Zhuangzi on the mind that reflects truly: it is a mirror. It conducts nothing and anticipates nothing; it responds to what is before it, but does not retain it. What would it mean for a soul to be that kind of mirror to the divine light?

sirach-we-may-speak-much-and-yet-come-sh.text: We may speak much, and yet come short: wherefore in sum, he is all. How shall we be able to magnify him? for he is great above all his works. The Lord is terrible and very great, and marvellous is his power. When ye glorify the Lord, exalt him as much as ye can; for even yet will he far exceed: and when ye exalt him, put forth all your strength, and be not weary; for ye can never go far enough

hebrews-he-sware-by-himself.text: For when God made promise to Abraham, because he could swear by no greater, he sware by himself
